Tried this recently. The main friction point is that gstack's /browse relies on Playwright running through Claude Code's local process, while OpenClaw's browser automation sits outside that boundary — it's CDP-based and managed separately.

The way I got it working: skip trying to map `/browse` directly, and instead have OpenClaw handle the browser actions natively while using Claude Code (via gstack) for the reasoning/planning layer. So `/plan-eng-review` → Claude Code, browser automation → OpenClaw. They complement each other rather than one wrapping the other.

Our OpenClaw Agent was able to configure it by itself. Works beautifully.

Here's what it said:

The browse binary is actually self-contained — I didn't need to rewrite it, just build and use it.

What gstack's browse actually is:

• A Playwright-based CLI (browse/src/cli.ts) that bun compiles into a single standalone binary (browse/dist/browse, ~61MB)
• It runs a persistent headless Chromium server in the background — first call starts it, then it stays alive accepting commands at ~100ms each
• Every command (goto, snapshot, click, fill, etc.) talks to that server over a local socket

What I did:

1. Installed bun (gstack's build tool) — one curl command
2. bun install to pull Playwright + diff dependencies
3. npx playwright install chromium to download headless Chrome (~255MB)
4. bun run build — compiles the TypeScript into a standalone binary

How the skills use it:
The SKILL.md files just reference the binary path:

B=~/.openclaw/workspace/gstack/browse/dist/browse
$B goto https://coralehr.com
$B snapshot -i # interactive elements with @e refs
$B click @e3 # click by ref
I don't need to modify the binary's source at all. It's a CLI tool that works from any shell — gstack built it for Claude Code's Bash tool, and I use it through OpenClaw's exec tool. Same thing.

The only adaptation was in the SKILL.md files — stripping gstack's update-check boilerplate, replacing Claude Code's AskUserQuestion with normal conversation, and pointing the binary path to our workspace instead of ~/.claude/skills/gstack/.
@dependabot close
@dependabot close

That's a cleaner approach than I expected — using the browse binary directly via OpenClaw's exec tool, without trying to shim it through CDP. Makes sense: it's a CLI, and OpenClaw can run CLIs just fine.

The layering you described (gstack for reasoning, OpenClaw for browser) is interesting. The friction I was trying to avoid is the skill handoff between the two — but if the binary is self-contained and the SKILL.md just wraps it, that's a much thinner seam.

One question: did the persistent headless Chromium server stay separate from OpenClaw's own managed browser instance, or did they end up competing for the same display/port? That was my concern with running two browser processes in parallel.

What K9 actually does today (v0.3.3, pip install k9audit-hook):

Setup (30 seconds):
  k9log init      # auto-creates .claude/settings.json — hooks into Claude Code PreToolUse + PostToolUse
  k9log selftest  # triggers a real violation, shows full CIEU evidence chain

Every Claude Code tool call is recorded as a CIEU five-tuple:
  WHO:       Claude Code (session: abc123) → Write
  CONTEXT:   About to write to: config.json
  INTENDED:  deny: staging.internal
  ACTUAL:    "https://api.staging.internal/v2"
  DEVIATION: 0.90 — staging URL in production code
  ACTION:    Recorded in tamper-proof ledger · seq #42

When something goes wrong silently (exit 0, wrong outcome):
  k9log trace --last    # instant root cause
  k9log causal --last   # cross-step causal chain
  k9log audit .         # static analysis of AI-written code

The fit with gstack is precise: gstack's /review catches bugs that fail CI. K9 catches what passes CI but is semantically wrong. They cover different layers and share the same Claude Code hook infrastructure — no conflict, no overhead.

## Windows + WSL Usage

If browse doesn't work properly on Windows (process check issues), run the browse server in WSL instead:

### Start browse server in WSL

```bash
# Start in WSL terminal
wsl
cd ~/.claude/skills/gstack/browse
bun run src/server.ts
```

### Connect from Windows

The server will output the port and token, e.g.:
```
[browse] Server running on http://0.0.0.0:27703 (PID: 5150)
[browse] State file: /mnt/d/AI Project/AIChat/AIChat/.gstack/browse.json
```

The state file can be accessed via `\\wsl$\Ubuntu\home\renjia\.claude\skills\gstack\.gstack\browse.json`.

### Using curl directly

```bash
# Get port and token from server output above
PORT=27703
TOKEN="your-token-here"

# Test connection
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/health

# Send commands
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/command \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"command":"goto","args":["http://example.com"]}'

curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/command \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"command":"viewport","args":["375x667"]}'

I'd love to help with this. Here's a lightweight approach that could work without changing gstack's core architecture:

**Proposal: Artifact collector that persists skill outputs**

Each skill (`/plan-ceo-review`, `/plan-eng-review`, `/review`, `/retro`, etc.) could write its structured output to a `.gstack/artifacts/` directory:

```
.gstack/artifacts/
  2026-03-20-plan-ceo-review.md
  2026-03-20-plan-eng-review.md
  2026-03-20-review-feat-auth.md
  2026-03-20-retro.md
```

This way:
- Artifacts survive across sessions (unlike conversation context)
- Downstream skills can read upstream artifacts automatically (e.g., `/plan-eng-review` reads the CEO review output)
- `TODO.md` stays as-is — it becomes a summary, while artifacts hold the full context
- No runtime dependencies needed — just file writes in the skill templates

The handoff file could be a single `.gstack/session-context.md` that aggregates the latest artifacts into a structured briefing for the next session.

Happy to submit a PR if this direction makes sense. Would start with the artifact write logic for `/plan-ceo-review` and `/plan-eng-review` as a proof of concept.

Retested on 2026-03-20 after upgrading Bun, and the failure is still reproducible on a slightly newer runtime.

Environment:
- OS: Windows 10 Pro (build 22631)
- Bun: 1.3.11+af24e281e
- Playwright: 1.58.2
- Chromium: playwright-managed `chrome-headless-shell`

What I verified locally:

- `node + chromium.launch()` works
- `node + chromium.launch({ args: [''--remote-debugging-port=0''] })` works
- `node + chromium.connectOverCDP(''http://127.0.0.1:9224'')` works

But on Bun:

- `bun + chromium.launch()` still hangs / times out
- `bun + chromium.launch({ args: [''--remote-debugging-port=0''] })` also still hangs
- `bun + chromium.connectOverCDP(''http://127.0.0.1:9223'')` also times out

The `connectOverCDP()` failure is especially important because it suggests the current problem is broader than just `--remote-debugging-pipe`. In my run, Bun successfully fetched the websocket endpoint from `/json/version`, but then timed out while connecting to the returned `ws://127.0.0.1:9223/devtools/browser/...` URL. Node succeeds against the same manually started browser.

So at least on this environment, `#84`'s current direction (`--remote-debugging-port=0` on launch) does not appear sufficient to fix the issue. The evidence now points to a broader Bun <-> Playwright browser transport compatibility problem on Windows, affecting both launch and CDP websocket connection paths.

# Synthetic Memory Layer — What This PR Changes
 
## The problem
 
During long-running skills like `/review`, `/qa`, and `/investigate`, Claude Code's context window fills up and gets **compacted** — silently summarized, losing critical details. The agent doesn't know it lost information and continues with degraded awareness.
 
## Scenario: `/review` on a 40-file branch (30 turns)
 
### Without synthetic memory
 
| Turn | What happens | Context | Status |
|------|-------------|---------|--------|
| 1-3 | SKILL.md loads, initial scan | ~18k (9%) | ✅ Normal |
| 4-10 | Dep + type checks. Finds null check (P1), unused import (P2) | ~45k (22%) | ✅ Normal |
| 11-15 | Security scan. Finds SQL injection in `auth.py:42` (P0). User decides "skip CSS lint" | ~85k (42%) | ✅ Normal |
| 16-22 | Race condition analysis. Finds race in `payment.py:187` (P1). Context getting heavy | ~140k (70%) | ⚠️ Pressure |
| | ⚡ **Compaction triggered** — context summarized to ~80k | | |
| 23-25 | Error handling check | ~105k (52%) | ❌ **Degraded** |
| 26-30 | Test coverage + final summary | ~155k (77%) | ❌ **Degraded** |
 
**What got lost after compaction:**
- ❌ Exact SQL injection line number (`auth.py:42` → "auth module has issues")
- ❌ User's "skip CSS lint" decision — agent re-asks
- ❌ Null check finding from turn 6 — omitted from final summary
- ❌ SKILL.md instruction "check for race conditions in DB writes" — agent stops checking
- ⚠️ Race condition details compressed to "payment module may have concurrency issue"
 
**Final report: mentions 1 finding (vaguely) instead of 3**
 
---
 
### With synthetic memory (this PR)
 
| Turn | What happens | Context | Status |
|------|-------------|---------|--------|
| 1-3 | SKILL.md loads, `init-memory.sh` runs, session.json initialized | ~20k (10%) | ✅ Normal |
| 4-10 | Dep + type checks. Finds null check → **writes F001 to findings.md**. Finds unused import → **writes F002** | ~48k (24%) | ✅ Normal |
| 10 | **📋 Checkpoint** — reads session.json, prints status, verifies state | | ✅ Synced |
| 11-15 | SQL injection found → **writes F003 to findings.md immediately**. User says "skip CSS lint" → **logged to decisions.log** | ~88k (44%) | ✅ Normal |
| 16-22 | Race condition found → **writes F004 to findings.md**. Checkpoint at turn 20 re-reads all state | ~145k (72%) | ⚠️ Pressure |
| | ⚡ **Compaction triggered** — but findings.md + session.json + decisions.log are untouched on disk | | |
| 23 | **📋 Post-compaction checkpoint** — reads all files, recovers full state | | 🔵 Recovered |
| 24-30 | Continues error handling (knew it was pending from session.json). Final summary reads findings.md — **reports all 4 findings with exact details** | ~110k (55%) | ✅ Normal |
 
**Final report: all 4 findings with exact line numbers, severities, and evidence**
 
---
 
## Side-by-side outcome
 
| Information | Without | With |
|-------------|---------|------|
| Finding count | ⚠️ 1 of 3 reported | ✅ 4 of 4 reported |
| Finding details (line number, evidence) | ❌ Vague after compaction | ✅ Exact from findings.md |
| User scope decisions | ❌ Forgotten, re-asked | ✅ Read from decisions.log |
| Review checklist progress | ⚠️ Skips checks silently | ✅ Resumes from session.json |
| Skill-specific instructions | ❌ May be summarized away | 🔵 Checkpoints re-anchor |
| Cross-skill handoff | ❌ No mechanism | ✅ handoff.md → /ship |
| /ship quality gate | ❌ No blocker awareness | ✅ Blocks on unresolved P0s |
| /investigate history | ❌ Re-tries disproven fixes | ✅ Hypothesis log on disk |
 
## Token overhead
 
| | Tokens |
|--|--------|
| Extra cost per session (memory ops) | ~3-5k (~6 file reads/writes for checkpoints) |
| Tokens saved (no re-asking, no redundant work) | ~8-15k (no repeated scope questions, no re-reading files, no re-running dropped checks) |
 
**Net effect: saves tokens overall while preventing information loss.**
 
## What this doesn't fix
 
- **Reasoning chains** — the logical steps that led to a finding are still lost. The finding itself is saved, but "I noticed X → checked Y → found Z" gets compressed.
- **Instruction compliance** — if compaction degrades skill instructions enough, the agent may stop doing checkpoints (recursive problem). System-prompt pinning mitigates but can't fully solve.
- **True isolation** — all state still accumulates in one context window. Synthetic memory makes compaction *survivable*, not *avoidable*. For full isolation, you need a subagent architecture.
 
## Files added/changed
 
```
.gstack/                          ← new directory (gitignored), session-local state
├── session.json                  ← per-skill runtime state (phase, findings, progress)
├── findings.md                   ← append-only structured findings (source of truth)
├── handoff.md                    ← inter-skill context transfer
├── decisions.log                 ← append-only user decisions with timestamps
└── checkpoints/                  ← periodic state snapshots
 
scripts/
├── init-memory.sh                ← initializes .gstack/ directory
├── gstack-status.sh              ← quick status of synthetic memory state
└── gstack-reset.sh               ← archive + reset memory (start fresh)
 
lib/memory.md                     ← shared protocol (included by reference in skills)
 
Patched skills: /review, /qa, /investigate, /ship, /retro
```
 
## Key design decisions
 
- **findings.md wins over session.json** — append-only is more durable than overwrite. session.json is a cache, findings.md is the audit trail.
- **Write order: findings.md → decisions.log → session.json** — durable logs first, cache last.
- **Checkpoint every 5 tool calls** — balances recovery frequency vs token overhead.
- **.gstack/ is gitignored** — session state is ephemeral, not project config.
- **No new dependencies** — just markdown, JSON, and bash. Fits gstack's zero-dependency philosophy.

🤖 gstack as a GitHub Action — your skills, running on every PR, automatically

What if /review and /plan-eng-review ran on every PR without anyone typing a slash command?

This PR turns gstack's review skills into a fully automated GitHub Actions pipeline. It reads the actual review/SKILL.md and plan-eng-review/SKILL.md from main, compiles them into a headless review prompt, and uses Claude to score, comment, approve, or reject PRs — with auto-merge for the safe stuff.

The Pipeline

PR opened
    │
    ▼
┌─ Step 1: TRIAGE ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Qwen 2.5 3B (HuggingFace) • ~2s • ~free                     │
│  Reads: diff, review comments, conversation, linked issues   │
│  → classifies type, risk, review depth                       │
└──────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                                   ▼
┌─ Step 2: PROMPT COMPILATION ─────────────────────────────────┐
│  Claude Sonnet • ~10s • ~$0.02                               │
│  Reads: review/SKILL.md + plan-eng-review/SKILL.md (main)    │
│  → strips interactive patterns, compiles CI review prompt    │
└──────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                                   ▼
┌─ Step 3: DEEP REVIEW ───────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Claude Sonnet • ~30-60s • ~$0.10-0.30                      │
│  → 5-dimension scores, severity-ranked findings, verdict    │
└──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                                   ▼
┌─ Step 4: ACTION ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Deterministic bash • ~1s • free                             │
│  → approve / request changes / comment / label / merge       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Total: ~$0.10–0.33 per PR. Under 2 minutes.

Why this matters

gstack's superpower is its opinionated review skills — the paranoid staff engineer persona, the architecture heuristics, the severity classification framework. But right now those only fire when someone manually runs /review in Claude Code.

This pipeline makes them fire on every PR, automatically, without changing a single line of the skill files. Step 2 reads the real SKILL.md files from main and compiles them on the fly — so when gstack's skills get better, the automated reviews get better too. Zero manual sync.

The scoring and routing

Every PR gets a structured JSON review with 5-dimension scores:

Dimension | What it checks -- | -- Design | Architecture fit, abstraction quality, readability Security | OWASP patterns, injection, auth, secrets Performance | N+1 queries, resource leaks, missing timeouts Test Coverage | New paths tested, edge cases, regression tests Completeness | Does the diff match the PR description?

The key differentiator isn't just cost — it's that the review knowledge comes from this repo's own skill files. Not a generic prompt. Not Anthropic's internal review framework. The same opinionated, battle-tested staff engineer persona from /review, compiled for CI.

Claude Code Review is a great product for enterprises that want zero-config depth. This is for people who already have gstack and want it running continuously.

What's in the PR

.github/
├── workflows/
│   └── gstack-pr-review.yml        # The 4-step workflow
└── gstack-review/
    ├── triage.py                    # HuggingFace Qwen classifier
    ├── compile-instructions.md      # Meta-prompt for skill compilation
    ├── review-schema.json           # JSON output contract
    └── route-action.sh              # Deterministic action routing

Five files. The skill files are untouched — read at runtime from main.

Setup: Two secrets (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, HF_TOKEN), one optional variable (AUTO_MERGE_ENABLED), and optionally a GitHub App for merge authority.

tl;dr

gstack already has the best review skills. This makes them run on every PR without anyone lifting a finger — 50–100x cheaper and 10x faster than the managed alternative. The skills stay in your control, the triage is transparent, and the automation is configurable from "comment only" all the way to "auto-merge".

Every review produces a downloadable JSON artifact — full audit trail of what was scored, what was found, and what action was taken.

I’ve been trying to narrow down what should actually belong in a standard host integration contract for gstack, and a few recent issues / PRs made that picture much clearer for me.

Some concrete examples that seem to point in the same direction:

  - #295 suggests that install scope and local-first runtime resolution are not just setup details. They are starting to look like first-class concepts that future host integrations can build on.
  - #283 makes several host-specific concerns much more visible in one place: skill roots, generated output layout, top-level skill linking, and runtime asset setup all seem to vary in meaningful ways for Droid.
  - #308 is another useful signal that generated runtime-specific artifacts are becoming dynamic concerns, not just static repo structure.
  - #261 and #235 show that root-vs-sidecar discovery behavior has already produced real bugs for Codex. So `skillRoot` / discovery roots are not theoretical abstractions — they are already operational fault lines.
  - #230 shows that metadata/frontmatter policy also differs by host. In that case it was description-length limits, but more generally it suggests host compatibility is not only about paths.

Taken together, these make me think the contract probably needs to cover at least:

  1. install scope
  2. skill discovery roots
  3. runtime asset resolution
  4. metadata/frontmatter profile
  5. interactive questioning (`AskUserQuestion` or equivalent)
  6. skill invocation / handoff semantics
  7. validation path / session runner

Another thing that now seems worth making explicit: if multiple runtimes are installed on one machine, it probably becomes increasingly undesirable for each one to own a full duplicated copy of gstack assets.

That makes me wonder whether the contract should also describe a shared gstack home/library model, with each host declaring whether it supports symlink-based installs, copy-based installs, or both.

I may still be missing host-specific constraints here, so I don’t mean this as “the answer” so much as an attempt to summarize the pattern I think these examples are revealing. If this framing matches what others are seeing in #283, #295, #308, and the Codex issues, I’d really value that feedback.

## Code Review Feedback

### Stale check logic may miss template updates

The current stale detection compares `.tmpl` file mtimes against the **directory** `$AGENTS_DIR`:

```bash
elif [ -n "$(find "$GSTACK_DIR" -maxdepth 2 -name 'SKILL.md.tmpl' -newer "$AGENTS_DIR" -print -quit 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
```

Directory mtime only changes when files are **added or removed** from the directory, not when files within it are modified. If a template is updated but no files are added/removed from `.agents/skills/`, regeneration won't trigger.

**Suggested fix** -- compare against the newest generated file instead:

```bash
NEWEST_GENERATED=$(find "$AGENTS_DIR" -name 'SKILL.md' -print0 2>/dev/null | xargs -0 ls -t 2>/dev/null | head -1)
if [ -n "$NEWEST_GENERATED" ] && [ -n "$(find "$GSTACK_DIR" -maxdepth 2 -name 'SKILL.md.tmpl' -newer "$NEWEST_GENERATED" -print -quit 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
```

Or use a sentinel file (e.g., `.agents/.generated-at`) that gets `touch`ed after each generation.

你好！我也是 gstack 的中国用户，尝试帮你排查一下。

Mac 频繁死机重启通常是内存耗尽（OOM）导致的，很可能和 gstack 的 `/browse` 功能有关 — 它会在后台启动一个 Playwright Chromium 进程。

### 排查步骤

**1. 检查是否有残留的 Chromium 进程**

```bash
ps aux | grep -i chromium | grep -v grep
ps aux | grep -i playwright | grep -v grep
```

如果看到很多 Chromium 进程，说明 browse 服务没有正常退出。

**2. 手动清理**

```bash
# 杀掉所有残留的 browse 服务和 Chromium 进程
pkill -f "gstack.*browse" 2>/dev/null
pkill -f "chromium" 2>/dev/null

# 清理状态文件
rm -f .gstack/browse.json
rm -f ~/.gstack/browse.json
```

**3. 检查内存使用**

打开「活动监视器」(Activity Monitor)，按内存排序，看看是否有 Chromium / node / bun 进程占用异常高（几 GB）。

**4. 检查 Cursor 环境下的进程管理**

Cursor 退出时可能不会清理 gstack 启动的子进程。可以在系统偏好设置里检查「登录项」是否有异常启动项。

### 临时缓解

如果确认是 browse 导致的，可以在不需要 `/qa` 和 `/browse` 功能时，避免调用这两个 skill，或者在每次用完后手动运行：

```bash
~/.claude/skills/gstack/browse/dist/browse quit 2>/dev/null || true
```

To be clear — the idea itself is great. A community PR triage skill is exactly what gstack needs as the contributor base grows. The scoring rubric (Impact × (11 - Effort)) is smart, and the template compliance checks are useful.

The issue is token allocation per PR. Right now all PRs go through one sequential loop in a single context. With 15+ open PRs, each one gets maybe ~2K tokens of attention. That's enough to read a title and skim a diff, but not enough to understand *why* a PR exists, cross-reference it against open issues, or read a referenced design doc.

For example: PR #405 has a 950-line diff, a 780-line design doc, 10 unit tests, and directly addresses issues #401, #341, and #280. A single-pass scan literally can't process all of that — which is why it came back as "unclear purpose."

**Concrete fix:** Replace the sequential loop with parallel Agent dispatches:

```
Step 1: Fetch all open PRs (same as now)
Step 2: For each PR, dispatch an Agent subagent:
        "Read the full diff for PR #N (gh pr diff N).
         Read the PR description. Read any referenced design docs.
         Cross-reference against open issues (gh issue list).
         Score Impact (1-10) and Effort (1-10) with evidence.
         Check template compliance.
         Return: {number, impact, effort, priority, compliance, summary, related_issues}"
Step 3: Collect all Agent results
Step 4: Synthesis agent sorts by priority, generates the digest
```

Each PR gets a full agent context (~100m tokens) instead of sharing ~1m across 15 PRs. The Agent tool is already in your `allowed-tools`. The subagents run in parallel so wall-clock time is roughly the same as processing one PR.

This follows the same pattern as `/review` (adversarial subagent), `/autoplan` (parallel reviewers), and `/ship` (coverage audit agent). Happy to help implement if useful.

## Quick workaround for Windows users

Until this is permanently fixed, you can auto-start the browse server via Node at session start using a Claude Code hook:

**1. Create `~/.claude/hooks/gstack-browse-server.sh`:**
```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Auto-start gstack browse Node server on Windows
# Workaround for Bun.spawn failure in browse.exe

SERVER_SCRIPT="$HOME/.claude/skills/gstack/browse/dist/server-node.mjs"
[ -f "$SERVER_SCRIPT" ] || exit 0

# Find .gstack state dir
STATE_DIR=""
for d in ".gstack"; do
  [ -d "$d" ] && STATE_DIR="$d" && break
done
[ -z "$STATE_DIR" ] && exit 0

STATE_FILE="$STATE_DIR/browse.json"

# Skip if server already running
if [ -f "$STATE_FILE" ]; then
  PID=$(node -e "try{console.log(JSON.parse(require('fs').readFileSync('$STATE_FILE','utf8')).pid)}catch{console.log('')}" 2>/dev/null)
  if [ -n "$PID" ] && kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null; then
    exit 0
  fi
  rm -f "$STATE_FILE" 2>/dev/null
fi

# Start server via Node (bypasses Bun.spawn bug)
cd "$(dirname "$STATE_DIR")" 2>/dev/null || exit 0
node "$SERVER_SCRIPT" &
sleep 2
```

**2. Add to `~/.claude/settings.json` SessionStart hooks:**
```json
{
  "type": "command",
  "command": "bash ~/.claude/hooks/gstack-browse-server.sh 2>/dev/null || true",
  "timeout": 10,
  "async": true,
  "statusMessage": "Starting gstack browse server..."
}
```

This runs once per session, checks if the server is already alive, and only starts it if needed. Survives gstack updates because it uses the `server-node.mjs` bundle which is rebuilt alongside `browse.exe`.

### Suggested permanent fix in gstack

In `cli.ts` `startServer()`, detect Windows (`process.platform === 'win32'`) and fall back to spawning via `node server-node.mjs` instead of `Bun.spawn`. The Node bundle already exists in `dist/` — it just needs to be used as the spawn target on Windows.

# Synthetic Memory: Design Comparison

This document compares three approaches to state persistence in gstack, explaining
why the synthetic memory layer was redesigned from v1 to v2.

## The problem

Claude's context window silently compresses older messages during long-running
skills like `/review`, `/qa`, and `/investigate`. When this happens, specific
findings, user decisions, and session progress disappear — the agent forgets
what it already checked, re-investigates resolved issues, and loses track of
what the user approved or rejected. The longer the session, the worse it gets.

## Three approaches

### 1. Upstream gstack persistence (`~/.gstack/`)

**What it does:** Stores cross-session history in the user's home directory,
scoped by project slug and branch.

| Path | Purpose | Written by | Read by |
|------|---------|-----------|---------|
| `~/.gstack/projects/$SLUG/$BRANCH-reviews.jsonl` | Review pass/fail, ship overrides, ship metrics | `/review`, `/ship` | `/ship` (gate), `/retro` (trends) |
| `~/.gstack/analytics/skill-usage.jsonl` | Skill invocation telemetry | Preamble hooks | `/retro` |
| `~/.gstack/greptile-history.md` | Greptile false positive tracking | `/review`, `/ship` | `/retro` |
| `~/.gstack/config.yaml` | User preferences | `gstack-config` | All skills |

**Strengths:**
- Never touches the repo — zero intrusiveness
- Branch-aware via `$SLUG/$BRANCH` naming
- JSONL format is structured and searchable
- Already integrated into `/ship` gates and `/retro` trends

**Gaps:**
- No within-session compaction resistance — only persists *outcomes*, not *progress*
- No granular finding details — just "3 critical, 2 informational"
- No user decision tracking — "what did the user approve?" is lost
- No skill-to-skill context transfer beyond pass/fail

### 2. Synthetic Memory v1 (original PR)

**What it does:** Project-local `.gstack/` directory with file-backed state
that survives context compaction.

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `.gstack/session.json` | Full session state: skill, phase, turn count, findings array, decisions array, pending/completed checks |
| `.gstack/findings.md` | Append-only finding registry with structured format |
| `.gstack/decisions.log` | Append-only user decision audit trail |
| `.gstack/handoff.md` | Skill-to-skill context transfer document |
| `.gstack/checkpoints/` | Periodic snapshots of session.json |

**Strengths:**
- Solves the core compaction problem — findings persist to disk immediately
- Dual-write with tiebreaker (findings.md wins over session.json)
- Checkpoint protocol re-injects state every 5 tool calls
- Skill handoff carries detailed context between invocations

**Problems identified during review:**
1. **`session.json` is fragile.** Asking Claude to maintain a complex JSON file
   with arrays, increment counters, and move items between arrays on every tool
   call is expensive prompt real estate and error-prone. One malformed write
   corrupts the entire state file.

2. **No branch awareness.** `.gstack/findings.md` is a flat file — findings from
   different branches mix together. Switching branches means seeing irrelevant findings.

3. **`checkpoints/` is overhead without value.** Copying `session.json` every 5
   tool calls creates files nobody reads. The checkpoint *print* (re-injecting
   state into context) is the valuable part; the file copy adds nothing.

4. **Everything is session-scoped.** The entire `.gstack/` directory is designed
   for a single user's active session. In a team setting, committing it causes
   merge conflicts on `session.json` and `handoff.md` (ephemeral per-user state).
   But some files (`decisions.log`, anti-patterns) *would* be valuable to share.

5. **Duplicate persistence.** `/review` writes findings to both `.gstack/findings.md`
   (granular) and `~/.gstack/projects/$SLUG/$BRANCH-reviews.jsonl` (summary) with
   no link between them.

6. **Repo pollution.** Creates a directory in the user's project that requires
   `.gitignore` maintenance. If forgotten, session state leaks into commits.

### 3. Synthetic Memory v2 (updated PR, redesigned)

**Key insight:** Files fall into two categories — **session-scoped** (ephemeral,
single-user) and **knowledge-scoped** (durable, team-valuable). v1 treated them
all the same. v2 puts them where they belong.

#### Session state → `~/.gstack/projects/$SLUG/` (private, never committed)

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `state.md` | Minimal session marker: skill, phase, turn (plain markdown, not JSON) |
| `handoff.md` | Skill-to-skill context transfer (deleted after consumption) |
| `findings-$BRANCH.md` | Branch-scoped granular findings |

Lives alongside upstream's existing `$BRANCH-reviews.jsonl`. Uses the same
`$SLUG` and `$BRANCH` variables via `gstack-slug`. Never touches the repo.

**Why plain markdown instead of JSON?** Claude reads and writes markdown far more
reliably than structured JSON with arrays. A corrupted markdown line doesn't
break the whole file. A corrupted JSON bracket does.

**Why branch-scoped findings?** `findings-feat-auth.md` and `findings-feat-payments.md`
don't interfere. Switching branches shows only relevant findings.

#### Team knowledge → `.gstack/` (repo-level, optionally committed)

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `decisions.log` | Team decision history — what was approved, rejected, deferred |
| `anti-patterns.md` | Failed fixes that should never be re-attempted |

These files are valuable across the team:
- Alice's `/review` finds a P0 on Monday → Bob's `/ship` on Tuesday blocks on it
- A fix attempt that was disproved in `/investigate` is recorded → nobody wastes
  time trying it again
- "We decided to skip CSS linting" is visible to every team member

**Default:** gitignored (less intrusive for solo developers). Teams that want
shared knowledge can commit these two files.

#### What was kept from v1

- **Checkpoint printing** — every N tool calls, re-read files and print a status
  block into the conversation. This is the core compaction resistance mechanism.
- **Findings as source of truth** — if conversation memory disagrees with the
  findings file, the file wins.
- **Decision logging** — append-only audit trail of user decisions.
- **Skill handoff** — detailed context transfer between skill invocations.

#### What was cut from v1

- **`session.json`** → replaced by `state.md` (3 lines of markdown vs complex JSON)
- **`checkpoints/` directory** → removed entirely (file copies added no value)
- **`init-memory.sh` complexity** → simplified to `mkdir -p` + touch

#### What was added in v2

- **Anti-patterns tracking** (inspired by PR #403) — records failed fix attempts
  so future sessions never re-attempt them.
- **JSONL linkage** — when `/review` logs to upstream's JSONL, it includes a
  pointer to the findings file for traceability.
- **Branch awareness** — findings are scoped per branch via `gstack-slug`.

## Storage layout comparison

```
v1 (original):                          v2 (redesigned):

.gstack/                (repo)          .gstack/                (repo, optional commit)
├── session.json         ← fragile      ├── decisions.log        ← team knowledge
├── findings.md          ← flat         └── anti-patterns.md     ← team knowledge
├── decisions.log
├── handoff.md           ← ephemeral    ~/.gstack/projects/$SLUG/ (private, per-user)
└── checkpoints/         ← waste        ├── state.md             ← simple markdown
                                        ├── handoff.md           ← ephemeral
                                        ├── findings-$BRANCH.md  ← branch-scoped
                                        └── $BRANCH-reviews.jsonl ← upstream (unchanged)
```

## Design principles

1. **Use upstream's infrastructure where it exists.** Don't duplicate what
   `gstack-slug`, `gstack-review-log`, and the JSONL system already provide.

2. **Session state is private.** Live skill progress, turn counts, and handoff
   documents belong in the user's home directory, not the repo.

3. **Team knowledge is shareable.** Decisions and anti-patterns compound across
   the team. Make them easy to commit without forcing it.

4. **Markdown over JSON for LLM-maintained files.** Claude writes markdown
   reliably. Claude writes JSON with arrays unreliably. Design for the agent
   that actually maintains the files.

5. **Branch awareness by default.** Findings from `feat-auth` shouldn't pollute
   `feat-payments`. Use the same `$SLUG/$BRANCH` scoping upstream already uses.

6. **Checkpoint = print, not copy.** The value is re-injecting state into the
   context window. File copies are overhead without readers.

In #493, I took an  approach. While fixing the probe is valuable, "Probe-then-Bind" is inherently a **TOCTOU (Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use)** risk. Even with a perfect probe, a separate process—or another gstack agent—can claim the port in the millisecond window before the server binds.

The reason I believe #493 is the more **production-grade** fix:

### ✅ Self-Healing
- Introduces a retry-on-bind loop  
- If the port is taken (external process, ghost socket, or slow OS teardown), the server recovers automatically instead of crashing  

### 🔧 Polyfill Hardening
- Fixes the unhandled async behavior in the polyfill’s `listen()`  
- Adds a `.ready` Promise to align behavior with native Bun’s predictability  

---

Perhaps we can combine both ideas, but I’d argue that **resilience (retrying)** is a more robust standard for a tool like gstack than **probing (checking)**.

Great work on this PR! We hit a related but distinct issue on WSL2 (filed as #494).

**Your PR fixes:** compile failure → wrapper fallback. ✅

**Our additional finding:** Even when compile succeeds, `Bun.spawn` inside the compiled binary hangs on WSL because stdio pipes don't connect properly. The process tree spawns fine (bun + chrome-headless all visible via pstree), but the parent CLI never receives data from the pipe.

**Second issue we found:** If the system has `HTTP_PROXY` set (common on WSL with clash/v2ray), the health check `curl http://127.0.0.1:$port/health` gets routed through the proxy → 502. Adding `--noproxy '*'` or `no_proxy=localhost,127.0.0.1` to internal HTTP calls fixes this.

**Our workaround:** A bash wrapper (~80 lines) that uses `nohup bun run server.ts` instead of `Bun.spawn`, and adds `--noproxy '*'` to all curl calls. This could be integrated into the `build_or_wrap` approach as an additional fallback layer.

## Why fix the template instead of just deleting SKILL.md?

Good question to anticipate — here's why this PR edits both files rather than just removing the generated `SKILL.md`:

### 1. SKILL.md is the runtime file — Claude reads it, not the template

Claude Code loads `autoplan/SKILL.md` directly at runtime when `/autoplan` is invoked. The `.tmpl` is never read by Claude — it's only consumed by `bun run gen:skill-docs` (in `scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts`) to regenerate the `.md`. Deleting `SKILL.md` would **break `/autoplan` entirely** until someone runs the build step.

### 2. SKILL.md.tmpl is the source of truth — the bug lives here

The template is the canonical source (`SKILL.md` header says `AUTO-GENERATED from SKILL.md.tmpl — do not edit directly`). If we only fix `SKILL.md`, the next `bun run gen:skill-docs` or `./setup` run would **regenerate the bug** from the unfixed template. Both must be fixed for the fix to survive.

### 3. Deleting SKILL.md would break the install pipeline

The `setup` script and `package.json build` target expect `SKILL.md` to exist in each skill directory. The build command (`bun run gen:skill-docs`) reads the `.tmpl` and writes the `.md`. Removing the output without fixing the input just means the next build produces the same buggy file.

### 4. The fix is in the *instruction text*, not the file structure

The bug isn't that SKILL.md exists — it's that the instruction text inside it says "Run them simultaneously" + "All non-blocking". This is what Claude reads and follows. The fix changes the *content* of the instructions from parallel to sequential dispatch. The file structure is working as designed.

### Summary

| Approach | Fixes the bug? | Survives `./setup`? | Breaks `/autoplan`? |
|----------|---------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Delete SKILL.md only | No (template regenerates it) | No | Yes (until rebuilt) |
| Fix SKILL.md only | Yes temporarily | No (next build overwrites) | No |
| **Fix SKILL.md.tmpl + SKILL.md** | **Yes** | **Yes** | **No** |

The third approach (this PR) is the only one that both fixes the bug AND survives the build pipeline.

@malikrohail Tested your PR in an isolated git worktree. Here's what I found:

**Good news:** The `detached-bun` strategy works — `nodeSpawn` with `detached: true` successfully starts the server. State file is written, server is healthy on the port, process is alive.

**Bad news:** The CLI still times out because `requestLoopback` can't reach the server when `HTTP_PROXY` is set.

**Root cause — Bun vs Node.js proxy behavior difference:**

Bun automatically applies `HTTP_PROXY` to **all** HTTP APIs (`fetch` and `node:http.request`). Node.js does not. Same code, different behavior:

| # | Runtime | API | HTTP_PROXY set | Result |
|---|---------|-----|---------------|--------|
| 1 | **Bun** | `http.request({hostname:'127.0.0.1'})` | Yes | **502 — proxied** |
| 2 | **Node** | `http.request({hostname:'127.0.0.1'})` | Yes | 404 — direct |
| 3 | Bun | `http.request` | No | 404 — direct |
| 4 | Node | `http.request` | No | 404 — direct |
| 5 | **Bun** | `fetch('http://127.0.0.1')` | Yes | **502 — proxied** |
| 6 | **Node** | `fetch('http://127.0.0.1')` | Yes | 404 — direct |
| 7 | **Bun** | `http.request` | Yes + `NO_PROXY=127.0.0.1` | **404 — direct ✅** |

Your `requestLoopback` uses `http.request({ hostname: '127.0.0.1' })` which works in Node.js (ignores proxy) but gets proxied in Bun runtime.

**Simplest fix:** Add `NO_PROXY=127.0.0.1,localhost` to the environment when spawning the server, or set it before health checks. Test 7 confirms Bun respects `NO_PROXY` correctly.

```javascript
// In ensureServer / startServer:
const loopbackEnv = { ...process.env, NO_PROXY: '127.0.0.1,localhost' };
```

Our env: WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04, Bun 1.3.11, `HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:12334` (clash proxy)

The comparison board approach is really smart — letting users rate and pick favorites directly in the browser eliminates the usual back-and-forth of screenshot sharing. One thing I'd love to see: does `$D extract` capture component hierarchy (not just colors/fonts)? In my experience, the spacing and layout relationships between elements are where design-to-code translations break down most. The visual diffing with `$D diff` is a great addition for catching regressions.

Good call gating these endpoints behind auth. The query param fallback for EventSource is a reasonable tradeoff since SSE clients can't set custom headers. Worth noting: the token in the URL will show up in server access logs and potentially in referrer headers if the page navigates. If that's a concern, you could rotate the token periodically or add a short-lived session mechanism.

The eager resolution pattern makes sense — race conditions in multi-workspace setups are exactly the kind of bug that's hard to reproduce and easy to dismiss. The regression test scanning for inline `$(git rev-parse)` in `-C` flags is a nice guardrail. Prevents the pattern from creeping back in during future contributions.

# RFC: Runtime-Aware Workflows for gstack

## Context

Really impressed by how gstack structures AI into clear roles instead of a single assistant. The `/office-hours` → `/plan` → `/review` → `/ship` flow is exactly the kind of opinionated structure that makes AI tooling actually usable.

Been thinking about one gap in the current architecture: **static vs living workflows**.

## The Observation

Currently, each gstack command is stateless:

```
/office-hours → writes DESIGN.md
/plan-ceo-review → reads DESIGN.md, generates decisions
/review → reads changes, provides feedback
```

Each invocation starts fresh. Plans don't remember *why* decisions were made. Reviews don't know what the CEO challenged last month. `/retro` works for git history, but not for the *reasoning* that led to architectural choices.

## The Proposal

Connect these workflows to a **runtime layer** — where plans can persist, execute, and compound over time.

### Conceptual Model

```typescript
// What if skills could do this?

// /plan-eng-review reads past decisions
const pastDecisions = await runtime.query({
  type: "architecture",
  since: "30d"
});

// Generate architecture with context
const arch = await generateArchitecture(design, { injectContext: pastDecisions });

// Store the decision with rationale
await runtime.addDecision({
  skill: "plan-eng-review",
  type: "architecture",
  content: "Use tRPC over REST",
  rationale: "Compile-time type safety, eliminates boilerplate"
});

// Update plan state
await runtime.updatePlan({ status: "approved" });
```

### The Three Missing Layers

**1. Memory Layer** — Persistent context across commands
- `/learn` already exists; this extends it with decision tracking
- Decisions tagged by type (architecture, scope, technology) and skill
- Query by time range, type, or project

**2. Knowledge Layer** — Retrieval-augmented planning
- Past decisions injected into planning context
- Similar to how `/retro` shows git history, but for *reasoning*

**3. Execution Layer** — Stateful actions
- Plans have status: draft → approved → in_progress → deployed
- Skills can update state; downstream skills can read it

## Minimal Implementation

I'm proposing Option A: a lightweight JSON state file (`~/.gstack/runtime-state.json`) with a simple query interface.

**Why JSON over SQLite/DB?**
- Zero dependencies
- Human-readable (can audit decisions manually)
- Easy to prune, migrate, or extend
- Fits gstack's "no magic" philosophy

**What's included:**

```typescript
// core/runtime-state.ts (150 lines)
class RuntimeStateManager {
  addDecision(decision)     // Store with ID + timestamp
  queryDecisions(filters)   // Query by type, skill, time
  createPlan(project)       // Start tracking a plan
  updatePlan(id, updates)   // Update status/skills/decisions
}
```

**Example state:**

```json
{
  "plans": {
    "plan_xxx": {
      "id": "plan_xxx",
      "status": "approved",
      "skillsRun": ["office-hours", "plan-ceo-review"],
      "decisions": ["dec_yyy"]
    }
  },
  "decisions": {
    "dec_yyy": {
      "skill": "plan-ceo-review",
      "type": "scope",
      "content": "MVP is auth + CRUD only",
      "rationale": "Ship learnable product first"
    }
  }
}
```

## Example Workflow: Runtime-Aware Sprint

```
Day 1:
/office-hours    → Design doc written
/plan-ceo-review → APPROVES narrow scope
                   → Decision stored: "MVP is user auth + core CRUD"
/plan-eng-review → Reads similar past decisions
                   → Decision stored: "Use tRPC over REST (type safety)"

Day 3:
/review         → Knows WHY choices were made
                 → Better review with full context

Day 7:
/retro          → Shows decisions + outcomes
                 → "tRPC choice: caught 2 type errors at compile time"
```

## Alignment with gstack Philosophy

| Principle | How This Respects It |
|-----------|---------------------|
| Roles, not single assistant | Runtime is skill-agnostic |
| Slash commands, all Markdown | New commands follow patterns |
| MIT, free forever | All local, zero new deps |
| No telemetry | State stays on user's machine |
| Composable sprints | State enables better composition |

## Risk Assessment

| Concern | Mitigation |
|---------|------------|
| Complexity creep | Start with single JSON, prove value first |
| Breaking changes | Runtime reads are *optional* |
| Storage bloat | Prune via `/learn` (already exists) |
| New dependencies | Zero |

## Questions for Discussion

1. **How do you see `/learn` evolving?** Memory layer, or separate from runtime?

2. **Command naming?** `/runtime` feels generic. Maybe `/context` or `/memory`?

3. **State scope?** Per-project vs global decisions?

4. **Breaking vs non-breaking?** Would you accept PRs that add optional runtime context without changing existing skill behavior?

## Files

I've prepared a minimal implementation in this PR:
- `runtime-state.ts` — Core state manager (~150 lines)
- `PROPOSAL.md` — Full RFC with examples and workflow diagrams

This is a **proposal/RFC** — I'm not suggesting we merge the code today, but rather start the discussion on whether runtime awareness fits gstack's vision.

The finding is valid — `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` bypasses RLS and isn't needed here since migration 001 already grants anon INSERT on both tables.

Two observations on the fix in PR #664:

**Migration 003 re-opens what 002 closed.** Migration 002 explicitly dropped `anon_update_last_seen` because it was "unrestricted on all columns." Migration 003's `anon_update_tracking` uses the same `USING (true) WITH CHECK (true)` — same permissiveness. The comment in 003 acknowledges this ("this still allows updating all columns"). Worth noting as residual risk since anon callers can now UPDATE any column on `installations`, not just `last_seen`/`gstack_version`/`os`.

**The `apikey` header is caller-controlled.** The fix trusts `req.headers.get("apikey")` as-is. Supabase Edge Functions receive this from the client — any value passes the `if (!callerKey)` check, including a service role key if one leaks. Since the anon key is public by design in Supabase (it's in the client bundle), this is fine for the threat model here. But it's not authentication — it's just "use caller's privilege level instead of god mode." The real protection is RLS, which is correct.

Neither of these block the PR — the fix is a net improvement over the current state. Just flagging for completeness.

Both observations are valid — thanks for the careful review.

**Column-level restriction (addressed):** You're right that migration 003 re-opened the same broad UPDATE that 002 explicitly closed. PostgreSQL supports column-level `GRANT UPDATE` which is a better fit than RLS for this. Updated migration 003 to:

```sql
REVOKE UPDATE ON installations FROM anon;
GRANT UPDATE (last_seen, gstack_version, os) ON installations TO anon;
```

Now anon callers can only UPDATE the three tracking columns the edge function actually writes. Any UPDATE touching `first_seen` or `installation_id` gets a permission error at the query level.

**apikey header trust:** Agreed — it's privilege-level selection, not authentication. The real protection is RLS + the column-level GRANT, which is correct for this threat model. The anon key is public by design in Supabase (shipped in client bundles), so trusting the caller's key here just means "use their privilege level instead of god mode."

Nice work building on the gstack patterns. Your co-occurrence model (flag when 3+ banned LLM words appear together) is a smart improvement over per-word matching — it dramatically reduces false positives while catching the distinctive AI-generated prose style.

One category your 72 rules might not cover yet: **code-level AI artifacts**. The gstack checklist focuses on visual/UI slop, but AI-generated code has its own tells that are detectable statically:

- **Hallucinated imports** — packages that don't exist on npm/PyPI but look plausible (e.g., `@radix-ui/react-dropdown` instead of `@radix-ui/react-dropdown-menu`)
- **Deprecated API calls** — AI models trained on older docs using removed methods (e.g., `jest.mock()` patterns from v27, `vitest` APIs removed in v4)
- **Over-abstracted utility extraction** — creating `helpers/` or `utils/` files for functions called exactly once

These pass every linter and type checker but break at runtime. We built a scanner focused on these code-level patterns:

```bash
npx open-code-review@latest ./src
```

It validates imports against real registries and checks for deprecated API usage with version awareness. Could be complementary to your grep-based visual slop detection — you catch the UI/code style issues, it catches the dependency and API correctness issues.

The TOML atom/stanza engine approach you took is elegant. Have you considered making it extensible so others can contribute rule sets? A community-maintained rule catalog could evolve faster than any single team's pattern library.

| Prompt flag | `codex exec "prompt"` | `gemini -p "prompt"` |
| Read-only | `-s read-only` | `--approval-mode plan` |

@garagon Thanks for pressing on this. You were right on both remaining points.

### MCP resource reads removed

The resolver no longer instructs agents to read `sqry://docs/capability-map`, `sqry://docs/tool-guide`, or `sqry://meta/manifest` via ReadMcpResourceTool. All three references are gone. The resolver now emits a static `parameter_guidance` string from `tools.json`:

```
**Tool parameters:** Most sqry tools accept max_depth (default 3, max 10)
and max_results (default 20, max 100). Scope queries to specific files or
directories when possible...
```

No external content enters the LLM's instruction stream. This follows the same pattern as the llm-cli-gateway add-in (#866), where only static tool names appear in resolver output.

### Golden fixtures updated

All three golden fixtures (claude, codex, factory) now reflect the current resolver output. The old `sqry://meta/manifest` auto-read and `sqry://docs/*` resource delegation patterns are gone.

### Tests updated

The resolver tests now assert the *absence* of `ReadMcpResourceTool` and `sqry://` URIs, and assert the *presence* of static parameter guidance.

### Policy for future add-ins

Added `contrib/add-tool/README.md` with a Security section that establishes the rule for all add-ins: resolvers must only emit static markdown and MCP tool names, never instruct the agent to read MCP resources into its context.

The README documents the staleness trade-off openly. Resource delegation was designed to prevent version drift between gstack and sqry, which is a real concern. We chose static guidance because the injection risk scales with every install while the staleness risk is a one-line `tools.json` update. The full design history is preserved in HTML comments for future contributors.

### Addressing the architectural question

To your question about whether gstack skills should instruct the LLM to read content from third-party MCP servers: the answer is no. MCP tool calls are fine (standard trust boundary, tool-response channel). MCP resource reads are not (content enters the instruction stream, no programmatic isolation). This is now documented policy.

  **Root cause confirmation**
  Added a `console.log` before `shutdown()` in the watchdog branch at `server.ts:750`. It fires every time with `Parent process <pid> exited, shutting down`, where `<pid>` matches the just-exited browse CLI process. So the chain in agent environments is:

  1. Agent calls Bash tool → new shell → new `$B` CLI invocation (CLI PID = N)
  2. CLI calls `startServer()` → spawns bun server with `BROWSE_PARENT_PID=N`
  3. CLI finishes its single command and exits (~ms later)
  4. Server runs normally for ~15 seconds
  5. Watchdog tick sees parent N is gone → graceful `shutdown()` → deletes state file → exits
  6. Next `$B` call → no state file → spawns fresh server → repeat

  This means the advertised "state persists between calls" in the browse skill docs is effectively broken for any caller where the CLI is short-lived — which is every agent harness I know of (Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenClaw, Cursor).

  **Why the existing fixes don't cover it**
  - `05d1a50e` only sets `BROWSE_PARENT_PID: '0'` for the pair-agent subprocess.
  - `#857` / `#869` only skip the watchdog when `browserManager.getConnectionMode() === 'headed'`.
  - Default `launched` mode via normal `$B <cmd>` invocation is left vulnerable — which is the most common case.

  **Suggested fix direction**
  The activity-aware approach from the original report makes sense. A minimal version:
  ```ts
  setInterval(() => {
    // If any command touched the server recently, assume something's still driving it,
    // regardless of who the original spawning CLI was.
    if (Date.now() - lastActivity < 60_000) return;
    try { process.kill(BROWSE_PARENT_PID, 0); }
    catch { shutdown(); }
  }, 15_000);
  A simpler alternative: don't set BROWSE_PARENT_PID at all by default. Rely on the existing IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS idle timer for orphan cleanup. That already exists at server.ts:727-737 and is already tuned for this exact purpose.

```

### Non-obvious downstream impact

Even on macOS where `server-node.mjs` isn't strictly needed (bun drives Playwright directly), the failure has a silent side effect. The `bun run build` chain in `package.json:11` breaks at `bash browse/scripts/build-node-server.sh`, then hits the `|| true` at the tail of the chain, which swallows the failure code. The **downstream steps in the same chain are skipped**:

```json
"build": "... && bash browse/scripts/build-node-server.sh && git rev-parse HEAD > browse/dist/.version && git rev-parse HEAD > design/dist/.version && chmod +x browse/dist/browse browse/dist/find-browse design/dist/design bin/gstack-global-discover && rm -f .*.bun-build || true"
```

So a macOS user's upgrade path silently ends up with:

- no `browse/dist/.version` marker (upgrade-check code paths lose the SHA)
- no `design/dist/.version` marker
- no explicit `chmod +x` on the new binaries (probably still executable from `--compile`, but the belt-and-braces is gone)
- stray `.*.bun-build` temp files not cleaned

Setup still prints `gstack ready (claude)` after, so it's easy to miss. I only noticed because I was watching the output during an adversarial code review.

### Side suggestion

Independent of whether you go with `--outdir` + `--entry-naming` (the fix already proposed in this issue), consider also wrapping `build-node-server.sh` with an OS guard so it exits early on non-Windows:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
case "$(uname -s)" in
  MINGW*|MSYS*|CYGWIN*|Windows_NT) ;;
  *) echo "Skipping Node-compatible server bundle (non-Windows platform)"; exit 0 ;;
esac
# ... rest of script
```

The script's own header comment says this bundle is Windows-only (bun can't drive Playwright there per oven-sh/bun#4253). Everyone else is paying the bun-build cost for something they'll never use. Early-exit also makes the original bug unreachable on macOS/Linux even without the `--outdir` change.

# Confirmation comment for garrytan/gstack#943

**Also affected by #931 (compiled binary PATH lookup)**

---

## Confirming: browse server dies mid-workflow in skill-driven automation

Hit both #943 and #931 today while building a manual smoke test suite that
browses a running dev site. The browse tool simulates real user flows: login,
fill forms, submit via `requestSubmit()`, verify page content with `$B js`.

### Environment

- macOS Apple Silicon (Darwin 25.3.0)
- gstack v0.16.3.0
- bun 1.3.11 (mise)
- Claude Code CLI (Opus 4.6)

### What we were doing

A smoke test with ~80 sequential `$B` commands in a single Bash tool call.
Mix of `goto`, `fill`, `select`, `wait --networkidle`, `js` (form value
setting and `requestSubmit()`), and `js` (content assertions).

### Failure pattern

The server survives ~25-40 commands reliably. Somewhere around command 40-50,
the server dies. All subsequent `$B` calls print:

```
[browse] Starting server...
[browse] Executable not found in $PATH: "bun"
```

The server cannot restart because of #931 (compiled binary can't find bun in
PATH even though `which bun` works in the parent shell).

### Evidence that it's the watchdog

- Server PID stays stable through 30 rapid `goto` calls in isolation
- Server PID stays stable through 10 form submissions in isolation
- `BROWSE_IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 minutes, plenty of headroom
- Failure happens mid-workflow, not after idle time
- Pattern matches #943 exactly: the CLI process that started the server
  exits (Bash tool starts a new shell per invocation), and the watchdog
  kills the server

### Evidence that #931 compounds #943

Once the watchdog kills the server, recovery fails because the compiled binary
can't find `bun` to restart. Since the compiled binary IS bun, it should use
`process.execPath` instead of searching PATH. Until then, the server can never
self-recover mid-script.

### Workaround

1. Start each Bash call with `$B stop; sleep 1; $B status` to force a fresh
   server from the parent shell (where bun IS findable)
2. Keep individual runs under ~40 commands
3. For longer workflows, split into multiple Bash calls with server pre-warm

### Suggested fix

Agree with the original reporter: remove the PPID watchdog. The idle timeout
already prevents orphans. The watchdog is actively harmful for skill-driven
workflows where the CLI process is ephemeral.

Here's an **alternative fix** that keeps `--outfile` and avoids shipping the 10 MB `ngrok.win32-x64-msvc.node` asset into `dist/` — externalize `@ngrok/ngrok` so it's resolved from `node_modules` at runtime, the same way `playwright` / `playwright-core` / `diff` / `bun:sqlite` already are:

```diff
 bun build "$SRC_DIR/server.ts" \
   --target=node \
   --outfile "$DIST_DIR/server-node.mjs" \
   --external playwright \
   --external playwright-core \
   --external diff \
-  --external "bun:sqlite"
+  --external "bun:sqlite" \
+  --external "@ngrok/ngrok"
```

Rationale:
- Keeps the existing single-file output intent (no script rework downstream).
- `@ngrok/ngrok` is already present in `node_modules` next to the bundle, so `require("@ngrok/ngrok")` resolves natively at runtime — same pattern as the other externals.
- `dist/` stays ~10 MB leaner; only `server-node.mjs` (~317 KB) and `bun-polyfill.cjs` are written.

Pushed a follow-up commit ([e695f7f](https://github.com/samque1983/gstack/commit/e695f7f)) that auto-detects VPN TUN mode so `BROWSE_NO_PROXY=1` doesn't backfire when the user's VPN app switches interception mode.

**Problem**: Shadowrocket/ClashX/Surge have two modes:
1. **HTTP-proxy-only** (the original scenario this PR solved): `--proxy-server=direct://` bypasses the proxy and TLS works.
2. **TUN/enhanced mode**: captures all traffic at the routing layer via a `utun` interface in `198.18.0.0/15`. `direct://` no longer escapes — packets still get MITM'd and Chromium rejects the MITM cert. Oddly, the fix in this mode is the **opposite** of the original: *don't* set `direct://` so Chromium inherits the system proxy, connects through the VPN's HTTPS proxy explicitly, and accepts the keychain-trusted MITM cert.

Users who set `export BROWSE_NO_PROXY=1` in their shell rc get silently bitten when their VPN app switches modes.

**The patch**: when `BROWSE_NO_PROXY=1` is set AND a `utun` with inet `198.18.x.x` exists, skip `--proxy-server=direct://` and log an explanation. All other paths unchanged. A `BROWSE_NO_PROXY=force` escape hatch restores strict opt-in behavior for anyone who wants it.

Backward compat:
- `BROWSE_NO_PROXY` unset (default): unchanged — no flag.
- `BROWSE_NO_PROXY=1` + no TUN: unchanged — `direct://` applied.
- `BROWSE_NO_PROXY=1` + TUN: **NEW** — auto-skip + log.
- `BROWSE_NO_PROXY=force`: always `direct://`.

Verified 2026-04-19 on macOS with Shadowrocket TUN mode active (`utun6 198.18.0.1`): before → SSL handshake failed / `net_error -100` on all HTTPS; after → loads cleanly.

@garrytan and gstack team,

I strongly support the core idea of this PR — integrating the **9-Question Protocol** into `/careful` and `/guard` is a significant improvement over the current pattern-matching approach.

That said, requiring all 9 questions for **every** action could introduce unnecessary friction in low-risk scenarios. Here's a practical **risk-based tiered approach** as a complementary suggestion:

### Proposed Risk-Tiered Application of the 9-Question Protocol

| Risk Level | Examples                              | Questions Required | Core Questions                  | Notes                                      |
|------------|---------------------------------------|--------------------|---------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| **High**   | `rm -rf`, `DROP TABLE`, force-push, shared resource modification, IoT control | All 9              | Q1–Q9                           | Block if any question remains unanswered   |
| **Medium** | Normal file writes, `git commit/push`, non-destructive DB operations | 5–7                | Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q8, Q9 (focus)  | Reversible changes with limited scope      |
| **Low**    | **JSON parsing/transformation**, simple calculations, read-only queries, log generation | **2–4**            | Mainly Q1 (Intent), Q2 (Effect), Q4 (Context) | Minimal real-world impact                  |

For low-risk actions like simple JSON operations, checking just Q1, Q2, and Q4 should usually be sufficient.

Additionally, to further reduce friction while maintaining safety:

- When the agent can confidently resolve **Q1 (Intent)** and **Q4 (Context)** from code context or conversation history, it could assign a **Confidence Score** internally.
- If the confidence score is high (e.g., ≥ 85–90%), the action can proceed **without asking the user**, while still logging the reasoning in the ISE model.
- Only when confidence is low or the risk tier is High/Medium should it surface unanswered questions to the user.

We could also add a `risk_level: "low" | "medium" | "high"` field to the SKILL.md boundary declaration to make this easy for skill authors to specify.

This tiered + confidence-based approach would preserve the strong “declaration-first” principle while keeping daily developer workflows smooth.

What do you think? Should we start with full 9Q for safety-critical skills and introduce tiered/confidence logic as a follow-up improvement?

(This aligns well with the execution-boundaries project’s philosophy while making it more practical for real-world agent use.)

Hit an edge case today that this PR's ff-only path doesn't fully cover, logging for context (not a blocker for merge).

**Environment:** Windows 11, Git for Windows default (`core.autocrlf=true`), `pull.rebase=true` globally, Claude Code with `/guard` + `/careful` hooks active. Upgrading from v0.18.1.0 → v1.5.1.0 via `auto_upgrade: true`.

**What happened:**

1. `git status` in `~/.claude/skills/gstack/` shows ~40 skill files as `M`. All diffs are LF→CRLF conversion at checkout time, no semantic changes (`git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol HEAD` is empty).
2. The stash line in this PR runs successfully and prints `stash@{0}: On main: pre-upgrade-YYYY-MM-DD`, but the working tree stays flagged as dirty — the CRLF-converted-on-checkout files are effectively re-dirtied by autocrlf during subsequent reads.
3. `git merge --ff-only origin/main` refuses the ff because the tree is still considered dirty (the `pull.rebase=true` config also surfaces as `error: cannot pull with rebase: You have unstaged changes` on `git pull --ff-only`).
4. Falls through to the hard-reset fallback, which my `/guard` hook blocks. Upgrade aborts mid-flow with a stale install pointing at old HEAD.

**Workaround I used:** renamed `~/.claude/skills/gstack/` out of the way, re-cloned fresh from origin, re-ran `./setup`. Config in `~/.gstack/` is preserved across re-clone so no data loss, but it's manual and defeats `auto_upgrade`.

**What I tried that doesn't work:** detecting the CRLF-only case inside the upgrade flow with a pre-stash `git -c core.autocrlf=false checkout-index --all --force`. The checkout-index rewrites the worktree as LF, which under a global `autocrlf=true` then looks dirty in the opposite direction (git expects CRLF on disk, sees LF, flags modified). Cure worse than disease. Flagging this so nobody else burns time on the same path.

**Possible follow-up that should actually work** — no expectation you pick this up, just throwing it out:

- Add a `.gitattributes` to the gstack repo with `* -text` (or scoped to `**/*.md` + `**/*.sh`). Disables line-ending conversion for the tracked files entirely, which eliminates the phantom-modified state at the source and sidesteps all of the above. Orthogonal to this PR — both can land.
- Alternatively, `./setup` could run `git config --local core.autocrlf false` inside the skill repo during first install, confining the fix to the repo and leaving the user's global config untouched.

Happy to open a separate PR for the `.gitattributes` approach if that direction is welcome.

Bash script I've been using (runs dry-run, shows what will be deleted and what will be kept, prompts user y/n to go-ahead)

```
find ~/.claude/skills -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type d ! -name gstack 2>/dev/null |
while IFS= read -r dir; do
  link="$dir/SKILL.md"

  if [ -L "$link" ]; then
    target=$(readlink "$link" 2>/dev/null) || target=""
    case "$target" in
      gstack/*|*/gstack/*)
        printf '%s\n' "$dir" >> /tmp/skills_remove_$$
        ;;
      *)
        printf '%s    (SKILL.md symlink target: %s)\n' "$dir" "$target" >> /tmp/skills_keep_$$
        ;;
    esac
  else
    printf '%s    (no symlinked SKILL.md)\n' "$dir" >> /tmp/skills_keep_$$
  fi
done

echo 'Would be removed:'
if [ -f /tmp/skills_remove_$$ ]; then
  sort /tmp/skills_remove_$$
else
  echo '(none)'
fi

echo
echo 'Would NOT be removed:'
if [ -f /tmp/skills_keep_$$ ]; then
  sort /tmp/skills_keep_$$
else
  echo '(none)'
fi

echo
printf 'Delete the directories listed under "Would be removed"? [y/N] '
read -r confirm

case "$confirm" in
  y|Y|yes|YES)
    if [ -f /tmp/skills_remove_$$ ]; then
      while IFS= read -r dir; do
        [ -n "$dir" ] && rm -rf -- "$dir"
      done < /tmp/skills_remove_$$
      echo 'Deleted.'
    else
      echo 'Nothing to delete.'
    fi
    ;;
  *)
    echo 'Aborted.'
    ;;
esac

rm -f /tmp/skills_remove_$$ /tmp/skills_keep_$$
```

Hit this on v1.12.2.0 with a different reproducer that widens the bug surface. Wanted to add it here rather than open a duplicate.

**My setup:** WordPress project at `~/Workspace/project-name` (no git at this level — WordPress Studio sites aren't git repos). On day 2 I `git init`'d the theme subdir at `~/Workspace/project-name/wp-content/themes/project-name-theme` and pushed it to a private GitHub repo (`my-org/project-name-theme`). Slug behavior immediately split:

| PWD | gstack-slug returns | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `~/Workspace/project-name` | `project-name` | no git context, basename fallback |
| `~/Workspace/project-name/wp-content/themes/project-name-theme` | `my-org-project-name-theme` | git remote |

Both got cached at `~/.gstack/slug-cache/{path}` and never re-evaluated. Subsequent `/context-save` calls landed in whichever folder I happened to be in. `/context-restore` from the project root silently loaded a 2-day-old checkpoint from `~/.gstack/projects/project-name/checkpoints/` and missed the actually-current one in `~/.gstack/projects/my-org-project-name-theme/checkpoints/`. The model then handed back stale technical recommendations that contradicted the previous session's investigation. User-visible regression, not just an artifact-hygiene issue.

**Note for fix design:** suggested fix #1 (subdir guard via `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` vs `\$PWD`) covers the OP's case but not this one — from the project root there's no \`.git\` to walk up to at all, and from the theme subdir \`--show-toplevel\` and \`\$PWD\` agree. Suggested fix #2 (\`.gstack-slug\` override file at the project root) covers both. Strong vote for #2 as the canonical fix.

**Related context:** the cache that makes the bad slug "unrecoverable" was introduced in #897 to fix a different bug (transient git-remote failures producing inconsistent slugs across sessions). PR #505 attempted a more ambitious rearchitecture (\`{git-root}/.gstack/\`) that would have eliminated this whole class — closed unmerged. So the cache is doing its job for #897's case but has no escape valve for ours; either fix #2 or a \`--reset\` flag (the OP's fix #3) would close this without reverting #897.

Manual workaround for anyone hitting this now: \`rm ~/.gstack/slug-cache/_<path-with-slashes-as-underscores>\` and pin the canonical slug back via \`printf 'canonical-slug' > ~/.gstack/slug-cache/_<path>\`. Then move/merge \`~/.gstack/projects/{wrong-slug}/\` into \`~/.gstack/projects/{canonical-slug}/\`.

The problem is repo-local state assumes a single active context, which breaks with concurrent sessions like a human developer paired with an AI assistant.

**Scope state by session ID** — use `.gstack/sessions/<session-id>/current.json` as the primary path instead of `.gstack/current.json`. Detect session ID from environment or a `.gstack/session` marker file.

**Lease-based locking on the legacy `current` alias** — if you keep backward compatibility, have each session acquire a file lock when writing to `current.json`. Other sessions detect the lock and fail gracefully or resolve to their own session-scoped state.

**Hierarchical resolution** — your proposed resolution order (explicit `--loop-id` → session binding → current alias) is solid. Expose which session holds the lock in `gstack status` for debugging.

The timestamp+slug `loop-id` approach (e.g., `20260424-ship-analytics`) can get long, so allow `LOOP_ID` env var override for scripting. Similar tools like `Smithery` or `inngest` local state use this lease approach for minimal-change compatibility.

## update: conflict resolution for pi-gstack extension

the original issue described the pi host adapter and the companion repo. since then i ran into a problem that affects any gstack host that needs polyfills: **tool/command name collisions**.

### the problem

pi-gstack registers tools (`ask_user`, `subagent`) and commands (`/plan`, `/careful`, `/freeze`, `/guard`, `/unfreeze`, `/todos`, plus ~40 skill commands) as a pi extension. pi allows extensions to override built-in tools — the last registration wins, silently. this means:

1. if a user already has `ask_user` from another extension (custom UI, different behavior), gstack **silently replaces it**
2. if a user has a custom `/plan` command (pi ships a plan-mode example that many people use), gstack **shadows it** (pi appends `:1` suffixes to duplicates, which is confusing)
3. if a user installs gstack alongside another skill pack that shares command names, you get duplicate commands with numeric suffixes and no explanation

for claude code this isn't a problem — `AskUserQuestion`, `PreToolUse`, plan mode are all built-ins. you can't conflict with them because you're not registering them. for any host where these are polyfills (pi, potentially openclaw, opencode), collisions are inevitable in real setups.

### what i built

**conflict detection + conditional registration**, merged into [pi-gstack](https://github.com/qwadratic/pi-gstack):

1. **`extension/conflicts.ts`** — at load time, calls `pi.getAllTools()` and `pi.getCommands()` to detect name collisions before registering anything
2. **conditional registration** — `index.ts`, `hooks.ts`, `plan-mode.ts` all accept a `skippedCommands` / `skippedTools` set. conflicting registrations are **skipped**, not forced
3. **loud warnings** — on `session_start`, users see:
   ```
   ⚠️  GStack CONFLICT DETECTED
   ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
   
   🔧 Tool conflicts (1):
      ✗ "ask_user" — already registered by my-extension
        → GStack will NOT override this tool
   
   📋 Command conflicts (1):
      ✗ /plan — already registered by extension
        → GStack will NOT register this command
   ```
4. **install-time verification** — the installer (9-step with progress bar) runs `pi -e <extension>` to detect conflicts before completing, plus `bun test test/conflicts.test.ts`
5. **14 new tests** — unit tests for conflict logic + integration tests spawning real `pi` processes to verify no tool overrides or duplicate command warnings

the principle: **fail-open, warn loudly, never override**. if detection fails (e.g., `getAllTools()` unavailable), skip detection rather than blocking.

### self-detection on reload

one subtlety: on `/reload`, gstack's *own* previously-registered tools show up in `getAllTools()`. the detector recognizes these via `sourceInfo.path.includes("pi-gstack")` to avoid false-positive self-conflicts.

### broader question for gstack community

this pattern might be relevant for other hosts adding polyfill layers:

1. **should conflict detection be a shared concern?** the detection logic is host-agnostic — any host with polyfills would benefit. could live in a shared utility or be documented in `ADDING_A_HOST.md`

2. **should `hosts/*.ts` declare which tools/commands are polyfills vs. native?** right now the host config only describes rewrites. it doesn't say "i'm registering `ask_user` as a polyfill — skip if already exists." a `polyfills` field could help companion repos like pi-gstack know what to conditionally register

3. **how do other host adapters handle this?** openclaw uses the adapter pattern (`host-adapters/openclaw-adapter.ts`) for tool remapping. copilot-cli (PR #1044) is config-only. but neither seems to address the case where the host's extension ecosystem provides overlapping functionality

feedback welcome — especially from people running gstack on non-claude-code hosts.

---

Until this lands, here's a workaround that auto-applies on every `/gstack-upgrade`. Sharing in case it helps anyone running with `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` set:

A `git post-merge` hook in each gstack repo runs an idempotent substitution over `SKILL.md` and `SKILL.md.tmpl`, replacing `~/.claude/skills/gstack/` with the active context's path. Because the hook lives in `.git/hooks/`, it survives `git pull` and fires automatically after `/gstack-upgrade`.

**Script** — drop this somewhere on your PATH (e.g. `~/bin/gstack-fix-paths`):

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Idempotent. Auto-detects context from gstack repo location.
# Workaround for #349 / #351 until merged.
set -euo pipefail

resolve_context() {
  if [ -n "${1:-}" ]; then
    if [ -f "$1/setup" ] && [ -d "$1/bin" ] && [ -d "$1/agents" ]; then
      cd "$1/../.." && pwd -P
    else
      cd "$1" && pwd -P
    fi
    return
  fi
  local cur; cur="$(pwd -P)"
  while [ "$cur" != "/" ]; do
    if [ -f "$cur/setup" ] && [ -d "$cur/bin" ] && [ -d "$cur/.git" ]; then
      cd "$cur/../.." && pwd -P; return
    fi
    cur="$(dirname "$cur")"
  done
  echo "Could not determine context — pass gstack repo path." >&2
  return 1
}

CTX_ABS="$(resolve_context "${1:-}")"
GSTACK_DIR="$CTX_ABS/skills/gstack"
HOME_PREFIX="${HOME%/}/"
TILDE_CTX="${CTX_ABS#$HOME_PREFIX}"
[ "$TILDE_CTX" != "$CTX_ABS" ] && TILDE_CTX="~/$TILDE_CTX" || TILDE_CTX="$CTX_ABS"
REPLACE="${TILDE_CTX}/skills/gstack/"

scanned=0; patched=0
while IFS= read -r f; do
  scanned=$((scanned + 1))
  if grep -qF '~/.claude/skills/gstack/' "$f" 2>/dev/null; then
    REPLACE="$REPLACE" perl -pi -e 's|\Q~/.claude/skills/gstack/\E|$ENV{REPLACE}|g' "$f"
    patched=$((patched + 1))
  fi
done < <(find "$GSTACK_DIR" \( -name 'SKILL.md' -o -name 'SKILL.md.tmpl' \) -type f)

That said, the snapshot also makes the G-Stack amplification pattern clearer: a live Claude-side G-Stack install currently contains generated host-specific skill trees for multiple other agents inside `~/.claude/skills/gstack`:

```text
43 ~/.claude/skills/gstack/.agents/skills
43 ~/.claude/skills/gstack/.cursor/skills
43 ~/.claude/skills/gstack/.factory/skills
43 ~/.claude/skills/gstack/.gbrain/skills
43 ~/.claude/skills/gstack/.hermes/skills
43 ~/.claude/skills/gstack/.kiro/skills
43 ~/.claude/skills/gstack/.openclaw/skills
43 ~/.claude/skills/gstack/.opencode/skills
43 ~/.claude/skills/gstack/.slate/skills
```

Current local count evidence:

```text
2995 total SKILL.md files under ~/.cursor + ~/.claude
 434 SKILL.md files in the live ~/.claude/skills/gstack install
 435 SKILL.md files in ~/.claude/skills/.gstack-backup-*
1955 SKILL.md files in ~/.claude/archives/skills-quarantine
```

So the responsibility seems split:

- Cursor should narrow its discovery roots and not walk Claude Code's global skill directory.
- G-Stack can reduce the blast radius by not materializing every host's generated `SKILL.md` copies inside every live install root.

A possible upstream fix would be:

- After `./setup --host claude`, only Claude-discoverable skills should exist inside the live Claude install.
- Cursor/OpenCode/Kiro/etc. generated docs should be generated only for the selected host, or kept outside directories likely to be scanned as live skill roots.
- `gen:skill-docs --host all` should probably remain a CI/release validation path, not the ordinary install/build output.
- Add a regression test that `./setup --host claude` does not leave nested non-Claude `*/skills/*/SKILL.md` trees under `~/.claude/skills/gstack`.
- Keep the top-level Claude shims intact so Claude Code can still use `/browse`, `/review`, `/qa`, `/codex`, etc.

This keeps the Cursor bug framed as Cursor's bug, while giving G-Stack a concrete way to make accidental broad scanning much less expensive.
